section.title: Nathan Rebukes David
section.sectionRationale: The LORD refuses to leave David's sin hidden. He sends Nathan, who traps David with a parable about a rich man who stole a poor man's only lamb; when David condemns the man, Nathan declares, 'You are that man.' David confesses, is forgiven, and yet is told the consequences will fall on his own house, beginning with the death of the child. The movement holds together God's justice and God's mercy, real forgiveness alongside real consequences, and it turns on David's genuine repentance.
section.thesis: God will not let His king's sin lie buried; He sends His word through Nathan to expose it, and when David confesses, 'I have sinned against the LORD,' God takes away his sin, yet the consequences of his despising God's word still unfold in his house, so that grace and discipline, forgiveness and lasting fallout, are held together in truth.
section.frameNote: Four beats: Nathan's parable and the verdict 'you are that man,' verses 1 to 12; David's confession and God's forgiveness with announced consequences, verses 13 to 14; the death of the child and David's response, verses 15 to 23; and the birth of Solomon and the capture of Rabbah, verses 24 to 31.

verses.text: Then the LORD sent Nathan to David, and when he arrived, he said, “There were two men in a certain city, one rich and the other poor.
The rich man had a great number of sheep and cattle,

but the poor man had nothing except one small ewe lamb that he had bought. He raised it, and it grew up with him and his children. It shared his food and drank from his cup; it slept in his arms and was like a daughter to him.

Now a traveler came to the rich man, who refrained from taking one of his own sheep or cattle to prepare for the traveler who had come to him. Instead, he took the poor man’s lamb and prepared it for his guest.”
David burned with anger against the man and said to Nathan: “As surely as the LORD lives, the man who did this deserves to die!
Because he has done this thing and has shown no pity, he must pay for the lamb four times over.”
Then Nathan said to David, “You are that man! This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you from the hand of Saul.
I gave your master’s house to you and your master’s wives into your arms. I gave you the house of Israel and Judah, and if that was not enough, I would have given you even more.

Why then have you {{bazah|despised}} the command of the LORD by doing evil in His sight? You put Uriah the Hittite to the sword and took his wife as your own. You have slain him with the sword of the Ammonites.
Now, therefore, the sword will never depart from your house, because you have despised Me and have taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your own.’

This is what the LORD says: ‘I will raise up adversity against you from your own house. Before your very eyes I will take your wives and give them to another, and he will lie with them in broad daylight.
You have acted in secret, but I will do this thing in broad daylight before all Israel.’”

units.label: Confession and forgiveness
units.note: I have sinned against the LORD

verses.text: Then David said to Nathan, “I have {{chata|sinned}} against the LORD.” “The LORD has taken away your sin,” Nathan replied. “You will not die.
Nevertheless, because by this deed you have shown utter contempt for the word of the LORD, the son born to you will surely die.”
After Nathan had gone home, the LORD struck the child that Uriah’s wife had borne to David, and he became ill.
David pleaded with God for the boy. He fasted and went into his house and spent the night lying in sackcloth on the ground.
The elders of his household stood beside him to help him up from the ground, but he was unwilling and would not eat anything with them.

On the seventh day the child died. But David’s servants were afraid to tell him that the child was dead, for they said, “Look, while the child was alive, we spoke to him, and he would not listen to us. So how can we tell him the child is dead? He may even harm himself.”
When David saw that his servants were whispering to one another, he perceived that the child was dead. So he asked his servants, “Is the child dead?” “He is dead,” they replied.

Then David got up from the ground, washed and anointed himself, changed his clothes, and went into the house of the LORD and worshiped. Then he went to his own house, and at his request they set food before him, and he ate.
“What is this you have done?” his servants asked. “While the child was alive, you fasted and wept, but when he died, you got up and ate.”
David answered, “While the child was alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, ‘Who knows? The LORD may be gracious to me and let him live.’
But now that he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I will go to him, but he will not return to me.”
Then David comforted his wife Bathsheba, and he went to her and lay with her. So she gave birth to a son, and they named him Solomon. Now the LORD loved the child
and sent word through Nathan the prophet to name him Jedidiah because the LORD loved him.
Meanwhile, Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and captured the royal fortress.
Then Joab sent messengers to David to say, “I have fought against Rabbah and have captured the water supply of the city.
Now, therefore, assemble the rest of the troops, lay siege to the city, and capture it. Otherwise I will capture the city, and it will be named after me.”
So David assembled all the troops and went to Rabbah; and he fought against it and captured it.

Then he took the crown from the head of their king. It weighed a talent of gold and was set with precious stones, and it was placed on David’s head. And David took a great amount of plunder from the city.

David brought out the people who were there and put them to work with saws, iron picks, and axes, and he made them work at the brick kilns. He did the same to all the Ammonite cities. Then David and all his troops returned to Jerusalem.

bazah.gloss: To despise, hold in contempt, treat as worthless. Nathan says David has despised the command of the LORD, and even despised the LORD Himself, verses 9 and 10. The word cuts to the root of David's sin: not merely weakness but a contempt for God's word, treating the Giver of everything as though His word could be brushed aside.

chata.gloss: To sin, to miss the mark, to offend against God. David's confession is stripped to three Hebrew words, chatati la-YHWH, 'I have sinned against the LORD,' with no excuse, no blame shifted. It is the turning point of the chapter, the honest naming of sin as sin before God, which David expands in Psalm 51 and which meets God's ready forgiveness.

basic.context: Chapter 11 ended with David's sin hidden and God's verdict that it was evil. Chapter 12 opens with the LORD refusing to leave it buried: He sends the prophet Nathan. Nathan tells David a story about a rich man with vast flocks who, rather than use his own, stole and slaughtered a poor man's beloved only lamb to feed a guest. David, not seeing himself in it, erupts in anger and declares the man deserves to die and must repay fourfold. Nathan springs the trap: 'You are that man.' He recounts all God had given David and charges him with despising the LORD's word by murdering Uriah and taking his wife. He announces lasting consequences: the sword will never leave David's house, and his own household will rise against him publicly. David does not argue or deflect; he says simply, 'I have sinned against the LORD.' Nathan announces that God has taken away his sin so he will not die, yet the child born of the sin will die. David pleads and fasts for the child for seven days, but the child dies. David then rises, worships, and eats, explaining that he cannot bring the child back but will one day go to him. God gives David and Bathsheba another son, Solomon, whom the LORD loves and names Jedidiah, beloved of the LORD. The chapter closes with the capture of Rabbah. It raises the questions of how God brings a sinner to repentance, how forgiveness and consequences fit together, and what true repentance looks like.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative that teaches profound truths about sin, confession, forgiveness, and consequences. Nathan's parable models how God's word can slip past our defenses to convict us. The chapter carefully holds together two things people often pull apart: God fully forgives David's sin, yet real consequences still unfold. The death of the child is a hard providence tied to David's sin, not a general rule that God takes children for parents' sins; David's confidence that he will go to the child, verse 23, has long comforted grieving parents with hope beyond death. The chapter is description of God's dealings with David, from which we learn about God's character.
basic.originalLanguages: Nathan's charge names the root of David's sin with the word bazah, to despise: David has despised the command of the LORD and despised the LORD Himself, treating the word of the God who gave him everything as worthless. David's answer is stripped bare to the Hebrew chatati, 'I have sinned,' no excuse, no blame shifted, the honest naming of sin as sin before the LORD. Between contempt and confession lies the whole drama of repentance, and God meets the confession at once with forgiveness.
basic.typology: Nathan the prophet, sent by God to expose sin and call the king to repentance, pictures the prophetic word that convicts and leads to life. David's confession and forgiveness, sin taken away yet consequences remaining, points to the deeper resolution in Christ, who bears not only the guilt but the full penalty of sin. And the child of David loved by the LORD, named beloved, in the line that leads to Solomon and ultimately to Christ, shows grace triumphing over judgment.
basic.christ: The gospel truth of this chapter is that God takes away David's sin, but Someone must still bear it. David is forgiven and does not die, yet the wages of sin are real, seen in the death that follows. This points forward to Christ, on whom the full penalty of sin like David's was laid, so that God could be both just and the justifier of the guilty. Nathan's 'the LORD has taken away your sin' finds its ground at the cross, where the sin was not ignored but carried by the sinless Son of David.
basic.god: God is revealed as both just and merciful. He is just: He will not leave sin hidden, He confronts His king through His word, and He does not pretend the sin never happened, allowing real consequences. He is merciful: He seeks out the sinner rather than destroying him, forgives immediately upon confession, and even names the next son 'beloved of the LORD,' weaving grace into the aftermath of sin. God is the one who sends the word that wounds in order to heal.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 51 is David's fuller prayer of repentance from this moment. Psalm 32 celebrates the blessedness of forgiven sin. Galatians 6 warns that we reap what we sow, as David does here. And 1 John 1 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive, the pattern seen in David's confession.
basic.oneStory: God will not leave His king in his sin; He sends His word to convict, receives David's confession, and takes away his sin, even as the consequences ripple through his house. This holding together of full forgiveness and real consequences finds its resolution only in Christ, the beloved Son of David, on whom the penalty of forgiven sin was laid, so that God is both just and the one who justifies the repentant.

context.literary:
Nathan's parable is shaped as a covenant lawsuit in miniature, the same three part pattern later prophets use at greater length, a recital of past benefits, I anointed you king, I delivered you, I gave you your master's house, verses 7 and 8, followed by an accusation, why then have you despised the command of the LORD, verse 9, followed by a sentence, now therefore the sword will never depart from your house, verse 10, the same rhythm found in the covenant lawsuits of Micah 6:3 to 5. The recital's repeated I gave stands in deliberate antithesis to David's own repeated taking in the previous chapter, so that God's generosity and David's greed are set word for word against each other before the sentence ever falls.

The parable itself is engineered for maximum emotional ambush. The little ewe lamb is described in almost domestic, filial terms, it shared his food and drank from his cup, it slept in his arms and was like a daughter to him, verse 3, language calculated to strike a father's protective instinct rather than a mere property owner's, which is precisely why David erupts in fury before Nathan ever mentions Bathsheba or Uriah by name. The irony sharpens on a second reading, since the story that traps David through outrage at what is done to a daughter figure precedes, by only one chapter, an actual crime against his own daughter Tamar, chapter 13, a connection the narrative leaves for the attentive reader to make rather than stating outright.
context.historical:
A court prophet like Nathan already had standing access to David, as 2 Samuel 7 shows, yet confronting an anointed king to his face over adultery and murder still risked the prophet's life, a risk later prophets like Elijah before Ahab, 1 Kings 18:17 to 18, would run again. The legal background behind David's self imposed sentence, fourfold restitution for a stolen sheep, reflects the law's actual penalty, Exodus 22:1, and many later readers have noticed, without the text ever stating it directly, that David's household absorbs something like a fourfold loss in the chapters that follow, the unnamed infant, then Amnon, then Absalom, then eventually Adonijah, though Scripture itself never draws this arithmetic explicitly and it should be held loosely rather than pressed as a formula.

David's mourning practice, fasting, lying on the ground, refusing food, was the expected posture of someone seeking God's favor over a sick child, so his servants' shock when he rises and eats after the child's death, verses 20 to 21, measures how sharply David's action broke with expected royal grief. Joab's careful message about capturing Rabbah's water supply, verse 27, reflects the standard siege tactic of cutting a city's water before its final fall, and his invitation that David personally finish the conquest, verses 28 to 29, preserved the custom that the glory of subduing a royal city belonged formally to the king, whatever the general's own part in winning it.
context.canonical:
The sentence, the sword will never depart from your house, verse 10, is not a single event but a program the rest of the book fulfills piece by piece: Amnon dies at a feast by Absalom's order, chapter 13; Absalom himself dies by Joab's hand while hanging in a tree, chapter 18; Solomon later moves against Adonijah, 1 Kings 2. What Nathan announces here as a word is carried out as a narrative across a decade of David's family life, so that the reader who continues past this chapter is meant to hear each later death as this verse coming due.

Yet the same chapter that pronounces judgment also secures the future king. First Chronicles 22:9 to 10 records the LORD's later word that the son to be born to David, a man of rest, would build the temple and reign in peace, language that reaches back to this very child, Solomon, born of this union and marked from birth as beloved of the LORD, verse 25. Nathan himself reappears at the very end of David's life to make certain Solomon, not a rival brother, actually takes the throne, 1 Kings 1:11 to 40, so that the prophet who once confronted the king over Bathsheba later secures her son's crown, grace and consequence woven through the same relationships to the very end.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wants readers to watch exactly how conviction is meant to work: not by direct accusation first, which David's own defensiveness might easily have deflected, but by a story that draws the hearer's own moral sense out of him before he realizes he has condemned himself, you are that man, verse 7. He is teaching, by demonstration, that the goal of confronting sin in someone with power is genuine repentance, not merely exposure or humiliation.

He also intends the reader to hold two truths at once without collapsing either into the other, that David's sin is fully and immediately forgiven the moment he confesses, the LORD has taken away your sin, verse 13, and that real, painful consequences still follow, verse 14, so that grace is never confused with consequence free living. And by devoting equal narrative weight to David's unexpected composure after the child's death, rising, worshiping, and eating, verses 20 to 23, the author means to correct any reader who assumes forgiven sin should leave a person permanently broken rather than able to worship again.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes one specific act of divine discipline, tied to David's own particular sin and standing as king, and it does not prescribe that every parent who loses a child is being punished for a specific sin, a reading the book of Job exists partly to correct. What the chapter does hold out as a stable pattern is the shape of true repentance, an admission stripped of excuse, and the shape of true confrontation of sin, a story or approach that lets a person's own conscience convict rather than mere accusation from outside.

David's conduct after the child's death, worship followed by ordinary eating, is likewise reported rather than commanded as a universal grief procedure; it is best read as one faithful man's particular expression of hope in God's future mercy, I will go to him, verse 23, not as a rule for how every grieving parent must behave.

debates.question: Why does the child die if David is forgiven?

views.label: Forgiveness removes guilt but not all temporal consequences
views.case: Nathan says plainly the LORD has taken away your sin; you will not die, so David's guilt is fully pardoned, yet the announced consequence, the child's death, still falls; Scripture teaches that God forgives freely while a sinner may still reap what he has sown, Galatians 6:7, so the child's death displays the seriousness of sin and its ripple of consequence, even as David himself is spared and restored.

views.label: A hard providence displaying sin's gravity, not a rule about children
views.case: Others stress that this is a specific, sovereign act tied to David's unique sin and role, not a general principle that God takes children for parents' faults; the point is the costliness of David's sin, publicly answering the private evil, while David's words in verse 23, I will go to him, hold out hope that the child is safe with God, so that judgment and mercy meet even here.

debates.bearing: Both agree the child's death is not a denial of David's forgiveness but a real consequence of grievous sin, and both find comfort in David's confidence of reunion beyond death; the chapter warns that sin is costly even when forgiven, while assuring that God's mercy holds, ultimately grounding forgiveness at the cross where the full penalty was borne by Christ.

debates.question: Was David's rising to worship and eat after the child's death exemplary faith or a startling break with expected grief?

views.label: Exemplary submission and hope
views.case: David's action models bringing grief straight to God in fasting and prayer, and then, once the matter is settled, returning to ordinary life and worship rather than prolonged despair, trusting God's future mercy and the hope of reunion, verse 23, a pattern later echoed when Job tears his robe, falls to the ground, and worships immediately after devastating loss, Job 1:20.

views.label: A startling reaction the text itself flags as unexpected
views.case: The servants are visibly astonished and question David directly, verse 21, suggesting the narrator wants the reader to feel the strangeness of the reaction alongside its faith rather than treat it as an obvious response; David's own explanation, verses 22 to 23, is offered as his personal reasoning, not as a divine commendation the way Job's worship receives no such surprised reaction from onlookers.

debates.bearing: Both readings can be held together, since the chapter records David's conduct with evident respect, giving him the final and coherent word, while still preserving, through the servants' honest confusion, the reality that hope filled composure in grief looks strange even to those closest to it, a tension worth sitting with rather than resolving too quickly.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter is stitched together by one small word repeated at every turn, dabar, meaning both word and thing or matter, so that the very language keeps holding together what has been done and what has been said. David has despised the dabar, word or command, of the LORD, verse 9; Nathan calls what David has done simply this thing, verse 9, the identical phrase the narrator used to close the previous chapter, the thing that David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD; and the child dies because David has shown utter contempt for the dabar of the LORD, verse 14. One Hebrew word carries the whole chapter's argument, that David's deed and the LORD's spoken word are finally the same kind of reality, and that despising one is despising the other.

David's own verdict on the fictional rich man exposes a second word worth noticing. He has done this thing and shown no pity, verse 6, from the same root behind the law's warning not to spare or pity anyone enticing Israel to false worship, do not spare him or shield him, Deuteronomy 13:8, and behind God's declaration that He will not spare a defiled Jerusalem, I will not look upon you with pity, nor will I spare you, Ezekiel 5:11. David unknowingly names, in someone else, the exact quality he himself failed to show Uriah, then receives back the very pity he had refused to extend, since Nathan's answer to his confession is immediate mercy rather than the fourfold death David had just pronounced.

Nathan's sentence introduces a third word that will govern the rest of the book, chereb, the sword, the sword will never depart from your house, verse 10. It is not a metaphor the narrative lets fade; it becomes the operative word across the following chapters, present at Amnon's death at a feast, Absalom's death in the forest, and the violent ends still to come, so that chereb functions almost like a title over the second half of 2 Samuel, first spoken here.

Finally, the name given to David and Bathsheba's new son deserves its own notice alongside the lexicon's treatment of Jedidiah. Shelomoh, Solomon, shares its root with shalom, peace or wholeness; a child born into a household torn open by adultery, deceit, and death is nonetheless named toward peace, before the LORD, through Nathan, doubles the promise with Jedidiah, beloved of the LORD, verse 25, two names laid one over the other, the parents' hope and the LORD's own verdict, both pointing away from the wreckage of this chapter and toward what God is quietly building through it.

typology.type: A story that draws self condemnation from the hearer's own mouth before naming him, 2 Samuel 12:1-7.
typology.fulfillment: Nathan's parable works by letting David judge himself before Nathan ever accuses him directly, a method Jesus later uses with religious leaders who condemn their own practice while judging others, for example the parable of the two debtors that leads a Pharisee to pronounce his own verdict, Luke 7:41-43. The pattern anticipates the deeper unmasking Hebrews describes, the word of God is living and active, and judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart, Hebrews 4:12, exposing what direct accusation alone often cannot reach.

typology.type: Sin forgiven yet a costly penalty still following, 2 Samuel 12:13-14.
typology.fulfillment: David is told plainly, the LORD has taken away your sin, and in the same breath that a real cost still falls. This holding together of full pardon and real cost anticipates, though it does not yet explain, how God can both forgive freely and remain just; the New Testament supplies the missing piece, God presented Christ as a propitiation, so as to be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus, Romans 3:25-26, the cost finally falling on the Substitute rather than further on the forgiven sinner.

typology.type: The prophet who secures the true king's throne against a rival claimant, 2 Samuel 12 and 1 Kings 1.
typology.fulfillment: Nathan, who once exposed David's sin, later intervenes at the end of David's life to make certain Solomon, the child of this very union, takes the throne rather than Adonijah, 1 Kings 1:11-40. The prophetic word that first announced consequence within David's house becomes, in the end, the word that secures a peaceable succession, a small pattern of God's ordained spokesman first convicting and then establishing His chosen king, one Christ fulfills completely as both the accusing Word and the enthroned King.

typology.type: The son named toward peace, born out of judgment and grief, 2 Samuel 12:24-25.
typology.fulfillment: Solomon's very name, sharing the root of shalom, and his prophetic second name, Jedidiah, beloved of the LORD, are given to a child conceived in the direct aftermath of adultery, deceit, and death. The pattern of peace being named and given precisely out of the wreckage of judgment anticipates the far greater child who would be called Prince of Peace, born into a genealogy that openly includes David's worst chapter, Isaiah 9:6 and Matthew 1:6.

study.christ:
Nathan's parable models, in miniature, exactly how the word of God still works on a hardened conscience, not by argument first but by a story that slips past David's defenses and lets his own moral sense convict him before the direct charge, you are that man, ever lands. Jesus uses the same method with people who would otherwise deflect a direct accusation, drawing a self righteous host to pronounce his own verdict through the story of two forgiven debtors, Luke 7:41-43, and Hebrews later names the deeper reality behind both scenes, the word of God is living and active, sharper than any double edged sword, judging the thoughts and intentions of the heart, Hebrews 4:12.

The chapter's central tension, David is told plainly the LORD has taken away your sin, verse 13, yet a real and painful penalty still follows, verse 14, is not fully resolved within the Old Testament itself. It states a problem the gospel alone answers, how can a just God simply take away sin without treating it as though it never mattered. Paul's answer, centuries later, is that God presented Christ as a propitiation through faith in His blood, so as to be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus, Romans 3:25-26. What Nathan announces to David as a settled fact, sin taken away, the cross alone finally explains, since here the guilt is pardoned but a penalty, the child's death, the ongoing sword, still visibly remains, while at the cross the full and final penalty is borne by Christ Himself rather than continuing to fall on the forgiven.

And the child born at the chapter's end, loved by the LORD and doubly named, Solomon toward peace, Jedidiah beloved, is the surprising, undeserved beginning of the line that leads to Christ, Matthew 1:6. A gospel that can trace the Messiah's ancestry through a child conceived in the direct wake of murder and adultery is declaring, before any doctrine states it plainly, that grace does not wait for clean beginnings; it makes its own, even out of a family's worst week, carrying the covenant forward toward the true Prince of Peace, Isaiah 9:6.
study.god:
God's justice and mercy meet here with a clarity rare even in Scripture. He does not wait passively for David to come to Him; He sends His own word through Nathan, actively pursuing the sinner rather than leaving him in comfortable silence, showing a holiness that refuses to let a beloved king's sin simply lie undisturbed. Yet the same God who confronts is the God who forgives the instant confession is made, the LORD has taken away your sin, verse 13, with no waiting period, no probation, no demand that David first prove his sincerity by a season of good behavior.

This God also refuses to let forgiveness erase consequence, which is not a contradiction of mercy but part of what makes His mercy trustworthy; a God who forgave sin while pretending nothing had actually happened would not be a safe God to trust with the truth about anything. The sword announced against David's house, verse 10, and the child's death, verses 14 to 18, show that God takes the abuse of power and the taking of innocent life with complete seriousness, even in the life of the man He loves and has chosen.

The chapter's most startling revelation of God's character may be verse 25, the LORD loved the child, spoken of Solomon, born into the very aftermath of adultery and murder. God's love here does not wait for a clean family history or an unblemished occasion; it moves toward exactly this fragile, complicated new life and calls him beloved. That is the same God who, throughout Scripture, keeps choosing to build His purposes through flawed people and damaged situations rather than waiting for spotless ones, not because sin does not matter to Him, this chapter has already shown that it does, but because His mercy is bigger than the mess sin leaves behind. He is, at once, the God David could not hide from, the God who forgave him the moment he stopped hiding, and the God who kept working forward, gently and deliberately, through everything that followed.

crossReferences.note: David's own fuller prayer of repentance, likely composed after this very confrontation, pleads for mercy according to God's loving devotion, asks to be washed and made clean, and offers, in place of sacrifice, a broken and contrite heart. The psalm supplies the interior voice this narrative chapter only reports from the outside, David saying I have sinned against the LORD.

David calls blessed the one whose transgression is forgiven and whose sin the LORD does not count against him, then describes the physical misery of unconfessed guilt, my bones wasted away, before his final admission brought relief. The psalm reads like a personal footnote on the very moment Nathan's confrontation broke David's silence.

Paul warns that God is not mocked, a person reaps whatever he sows, sowing to the flesh reaps corruption while sowing to the Spirit reaps eternal life. David's forgiven sin still produces a harvest of sorrow in his household, the sword that will not depart, verse 10, a sober, concrete case of the very principle Paul later states as a general law.

If we confess our sins, John writes, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. David's own bare confession, I have sinned against the LORD, and Nathan's immediate reply, the LORD has taken away your sin, is this promise in action centuries before John states it as a settled pattern for every believer.

Decades later Nathan reappears, this time to make sure Bathsheba's son actually receives the throne David had promised him, outmaneuvering Adonijah's attempt to seize it first. The prophet who once confronted the king over this very child's mother now secures that child's crown, grace and consequence still working themselves out through the same small circle of people.

The LORD later tells David that the son to be born to him, a man of rest, will build the temple and be given peace and quiet during his reign, language that reaches back to Solomon, born of this union and marked from birth as beloved of the LORD. The child conceived in judgment becomes the child chosen for the temple.

Jesus tells a Pharisee a brief story about two debtors, one forgiven much and one forgiven little, and lets the man pronounce his own correct verdict before applying it to him directly. The method is exactly Nathan's, a story that draws self judgment from the hearer before the direct application ever arrives.

The word of God is living and active, sharper than any double edged sword, piercing to the point of division of soul and spirit, and judging the thoughts and intentions of the heart. Nathan's parable is a small, dramatic demonstration of exactly this kind of word, cutting past David's defenses to expose what he could not see about himself.

Paul explains how God can be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus, since Christ's blood satisfies the justice that sin requires. This chapter states the problem in miniature, sin taken away yet a penalty still following, that the cross alone finally and fully resolves.

After devastating loss, Job tears his robe, falls to the ground, and worships, saying the LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away, blessed be the name of the LORD. David's own rising to worship after his son's death, verse 20, follows the same startling pattern of grief answered immediately with worship rather than prolonged despair.

The law requires a thief who has slaughtered a stolen sheep to repay four sheep for the one, the very penalty David pronounces on the man in Nathan's story without recognizing he has just sentenced himself. The fourfold figure he names is not invented drama but real, familiar law he knew by heart.

Israel's law warns against showing pity to anyone who entices the people toward false worship, do not spare him or shield him. David condemns the rich man in Nathan's parable for showing no such pity to the poor man, an accusation that returns on David himself, since it was exactly the pity he failed to show Uriah.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's whole account of redemption depends on a God who will not leave sin buried, and this chapter is one of its clearest small scale pictures of how that redemption actually works, exposure, honest confession, immediate pardon, and yet real consequence still unfolding within a world sin has genuinely damaged. Every later act of gospel proclamation, expose what is hidden, call for honest confession, offer free forgiveness, walks the same road first mapped out here between Nathan and David.

The chapter also answers, and complicates, the covenant hope running through the whole Old Testament. David's line was promised an everlasting throne, 2 Samuel 7:12-16, and this chapter shows that promise surviving the worst possible test, David's own gravest sin does not cancel it, yet the promise's fulfillment will clearly require more than David's own righteousness to sustain it, since the man to whom it was given cannot even keep himself from murder and adultery. The birth of Solomon at the chapter's end, named toward peace, called beloved by the LORD, is both a fresh mercy and a quiet reminder that whatever king finally secures this covenant forever will have to be greater than David, not merely descended from him.

The pattern set here, forgiveness that does not erase consequence, keeps recurring until it reaches its full resolution in Christ, where at last the consequence itself, and not merely its announcement, is fully absorbed rather than passed forward into another generation. What Nathan announces and David experiences in part, sin genuinely taken away and yet a real cost still following someone, the cross completes without remainder, the cost falling entirely on the Substitute, so that everyone who confesses as plainly as David did, I have sinned against the LORD, may receive what David received, forgiveness, and more than David received, since in Christ the debt itself, not only its guilt, is finally paid in full.

quiz.q: How does Nathan bring David to see his own sin?

options.text: He tells a parable about a rich man stealing a poor man's only lamb, and after David condemns the man, declares, 'You are that man.'
options.note: Verses 1-7 show Nathan's parable drawing David's own judgment onto himself.

options.text: He openly accuses David of adultery and murder from the start.
options.note: Nathan does confront David directly, but only after the parable has led David to condemn himself.

options.text: He uses a story that leads David to pronounce judgment on himself unawares.
options.note: True, but this option omits the dramatic turn 'you are that man' that makes the confrontation land.

options.text: He waits silently until David confesses on his own.
options.note: Nathan actively confronts David with a parable and a direct charge; David does not confess unprompted.

quiz.q: What is the root of David's sin according to Nathan?

options.text: He despised the command of the LORD, and despised the LORD Himself, treating God's word as worthless.
options.note: Verses 9-10 name David's contempt for God's word as the root of his sin.

options.text: He simply gave in to a moment of weakness he could not help.
options.note: Nathan calls it despising the LORD, not an unavoidable weakness.

options.text: He disregarded God's word despite all God had given him.
options.note: True, but this option omits the sharp charge that David despised the LORD Himself, not only His command.

options.text: He failed to consult the LORD before acting.
options.note: The issue is contempt for God's known command, not merely a failure to inquire.

quiz.q: How does God respond to David's confession, 'I have sinned against the LORD'?

options.text: He takes away David's sin so he will not die, yet announces that real consequences will still fall on his house.
options.note: Verses 13-14 hold together full forgiveness and real consequences.

options.text: He withholds forgiveness until David proves his repentance over time.
options.note: Forgiveness is immediate upon confession; God does not make David earn it.

options.text: He forgives David freely but lets consequences remain.
options.note: True, but this option omits the specific assurance 'you will not die' and the announced consequences to his house.

options.text: He forgives David and removes every consequence of the sin.
options.note: God forgives but does not remove all consequences; the child dies and the sword remains in David's house.

quiz.q: How does David respond after the child dies?

options.text: He rises, worships, and eats, saying he cannot bring the child back but will one day go to him.
options.note: Verses 20-23 show David's worship and his hope of reunion beyond death.

options.text: He refuses to accept the child's death and continues fasting in despair.
options.note: The opposite; David stops fasting once the child dies and worships God.

options.text: He gets up, worships God, and returns to eating.
options.note: True, but this option omits David's striking words of hope, 'I will go to him, but he will not return to me.'

options.text: He blames God for taking the child and turns away in anger.
options.note: David worships rather than blaming God, submitting to God's will with hope.

quiz.q: How does the chapter hold together God's justice and mercy in a way that points to Christ?

options.text: God forgives David yet the penalty is real, foreshadowing Christ who bore the full penalty of forgiven sin so God is just and justifier.
options.note: The pattern of sin taken away yet penalty borne points to the cross, Romans 3:26.

options.text: It shows that God forgives sin without any cost to anyone.
options.note: The chapter shows sin has real cost; ultimately the cost is borne by Christ, not ignored.

options.text: It reveals a God who is both just in judging sin and merciful in forgiving the repentant.
options.note: True, but this option stops short of the gospel resolution that Christ bears the penalty of forgiven sin.

options.text: It teaches that repentance alone fully satisfies God's justice apart from any atonement.
options.note: David's forgiveness is grounded, in the whole Bible's testimony, in the atonement Christ provides, not in repentance apart from it.

quiz.q: What does the birth and naming of Solomon reveal after this dark episode?

options.text: That God's grace and covenant faithfulness continue, as the LORD loves the child and names him Jedidiah, beloved of the LORD.
options.note: Verses 24-25 show grace triumphing, the covenant line carried on in the beloved Solomon.

options.text: That David's sin had permanently forfeited God's covenant promises.
options.note: The opposite; God's covenant continues, and the beloved Solomon carries the line toward Christ.

options.text: That God still blesses David's house despite his sin.
options.note: True, but this option omits the striking detail that the LORD loved the child and gave him the name Jedidiah.

options.text: That Solomon's birth simply replaced the child who had died.
options.note: Solomon is more than a replacement; he is the beloved of the LORD who carries the covenant promise forward.

questions: Nathan's parable slipped past David's defenses so he judged himself. Are there sins you readily condemn in others while excusing the same thing in yourself?
David's confession was stripped bare: 'I have sinned against the LORD,' with no excuse. What would it look like for you to confess a sin that plainly, without blame shifting?
God forgave David fully, yet consequences still unfolded. How do you hold on to the reality of God's complete forgiveness even while living with the fallout of past sin?
David rose, worshiped, and rested in the hope that he would go to his child. How does the hope of God's mercy beyond death steady you in grief and loss?
God wove grace into the aftermath of David's sin, naming Solomon 'beloved of the LORD.' Where have you seen God bring unexpected grace out of a season marked by your failure?

translationNotes.note: The BSB follows the Dead Sea Scrolls reading 'you have shown utter contempt for the word of the LORD,' while the Masoretic Text reads 'you have brought utter contempt from the enemies of the LORD'; either way the sin gave occasion for contempt toward God.

David's words 'I will go to him, but he will not return to me' express hope of reunion beyond death, long a comfort to grieving parents, resting in the mercy of God rather than presuming on David's own merit.
The BSB footnote explains that Jedidiah means 'beloved of the LORD'; the name given to Solomon signals God's love and covenant favor resting on the child despite the sin that preceded his birth.
